packs.title: Homes, collections and open paths
packs.promise: Follow city histories, look closely at living and art collections, and make room for a short outdoor return.

q.s: Build a field note from pattern, behavior and lifecycle.
st: Enter the open Butterfly House through its visitor doors and follow staff instructions. Choose a butterfly you can observe from the path without pursuing or touching it.
Write one visible wing-pattern detail and one observed behavior, including resting. Use an available identification guide if you want a species name; otherwise leave the name unknown.
Read the Emerging Wonders interpretation or another open lifecycle display. Add one stated lifecycle fact and identify the display that supports it; an emergence is not guaranteed.
Put the three records together: pattern, behavior and lifecycle. Mark which came from your observation and which came from interpretation.

q.s: Test a curatorial idea against two details you can see.
st: Enter an open exhibition at the Art Museum. Read its current introductory text or title and choose one idea or question it raises.
Choose one actual artwork in that exhibition. Record its displayed title and artist where supplied, then find two visible details relevant to your chosen idea.
Check the label or curatorial text again. Separate what it states from the connection you are making; a missing explanation can remain a question.
Write a three-part note: the exhibition idea, your two visual details, and the connection or question those details suggest. Do not assume a particular past exhibition remains on view.

q.s: Make a short storyboard from a booked lemur visit.
st: On your reserved General Tour, follow the permitted visitor path or your guide. Observe a lemur without trying to attract its attention; resting or remaining out of view is a valid observation.

Make three brief observation records during permitted stops or immediately afterward. Note a posture, a change over time, and one habitat feature or educator explanation. Record absence or uncertainty honestly.
Turn your records into three original written panels or small sketches with captions: what you first noticed, what changed or stayed still, and what you learned.
Add one line identifying a direct observation and one identifying an educator or interpretive source. This is your storyboard, not an invented account of the animal’s thoughts.

packs.title: Two downtown afternoons
packs.promise: Connect warehouse streets, public galleries, local history and a park through two walking afternoons.

q.s: Place three museum facts in order.
st: Enter the open museum and choose accessible Durham history interpretation. Look for three actual records with a date or stated sequence, using open permanent or rotating displays.
For each record, note a date or sequence cue, a person or community actually named, and the display or touchscreen entry that supports it. Do not supply a missing name.
Arrange your three records in chronological order. Mark an uncertain date or relative sequence honestly.
Write one question suggested by a gap between the records. Your timeline can be small; it should be grounded in the interpretation you read.

q.s: Collect what changed between two views of one work.
st: Enter an open public gallery and choose one actual work. Look for about half a minute before reading its label, then record two visible details and your first question.
Read the displayed label and any nearby curatorial text. Record one stated fact that adds context, such as its medium, title or artist’s subject.
Look at the same work again from a permitted distance. Find one detail you missed or one earlier observation that you would now describe differently.
Write a before-and-after note identifying the visible detail and the label fact that changed your attention. It is fine if your first reading stayed the same.

q.s: Make a small sequence from the exterior’s rhythm.
st: From a permitted exterior view, find a repeating feature in the restored mill building, such as a run of windows or brick divisions. Record three changes within that repetition.
Read the Golden Belt history link about the textile mill’s later reuse. Note one stated past use and one present use without assuming every door is public.

Make three original sketch panels or written scene descriptions: repetition, a change in the pattern, and the building’s relationship to the street. Give each panel a caption based on something visible.
Revise one panel to make its spatial detail clearer. Keep historical source notes separate from your own compositions.
